### ☐ `fact.how_money_works.oppcost_definition`: unverified

> **Claim:** Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative: what you give up when you make a choice.

- **Concept:** Opportunity cost (`concept.how_money_works.oppcost_definition`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L15 “Opportunity Cost” · `card.how_money_works.015.c2` (text): The price tag you don't see / Every choice has a cost that never shows up on a receipt. Economists call it opportunity cost: the value of the next best alternative, the thing you gave up by choosing. Sleep through a class and the cost isn't money. It's the learning you missed. Pick pizza for dinner and the cost is the burger you didn't have.
  - L18 “Small Costs Add Up” · `card.how_money_works.018.c4` (fact): $5 a day sounds like nothing. $1,250 a year sounds like a vacation. / An economics textbook example: spending $5 a day more on a bought lunch than one from home adds up to $1,250 over 250 workdays, perhaps the cost of a decent vacation. That's Level 15's opportunity cost, scaled up. Describing the cost as "a nice vacation" instead of "$5 a day" might lead to a different choice.
  - L20 “Checkpoint: Earning and Spending” · `card.how_money_works.020.c4` (text): Chapter 2 in one paycheck / Follow one paycheck. It starts as wages, the income labor earns. Deductions shrink gross pay to net. A 50/30/20 budget splits the net into needs, wants and saving, and every choice gives up the next best thing. At the till, price cues nudge you, card fees hide inside prices, small charges quietly add up, and scammers pretend, press and ask for gift cards.
- **Tested by:**
  - L15 `question.how_money_works.015.q1`: What is opportunity cost? → **The value of the next best alternative you give up**
  - L16 `question.how_money_works.016.q3`: From Level 15: a 9-ending price nudges you to spend $39. What do economists call the next best thing that money could have bought? → **Its opportunity cost**
  - L18 `question.how_money_works.018.q3`: From Level 15: in the lunch example, what is the opportunity cost of buying lunch out all year? → **The vacation the $1,250 could have paid for**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. OpenStax: in short, opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative. St. Louis Fed: the value of the next-best alternative when a decision is made; it is what is given up. Econlib defines it the same way. Sources: https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/2-1-how-individuals-make-choices-based-on-their-budget-constraint, https://www.stlouisfed.org/open-vault/2020/january/real-life-examples-opportunity-cost, https://www.econlib.org/library/Topics/College/opportunitycost.html

### ☐ `fact.how_money_works.oppcost_movies_time`: unverified

> **Claim:** A student who spends 3 hours and $20 at the movies the night before an exam gives up study time as well as the money.

- **Concept:** Opportunity cost (`concept.how_money_works.oppcost_definition`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L15 “Opportunity Cost” · `card.how_money_works.015.c4` (fact): Time is part of the price of everything. / Spend 3 hours and $20 at the movies the night before an exam, and the cost isn't just the $20. It's also the study time you gave up. So even when a lunch is free, the hour you spend on it isn't. That's the saloon lesson: there's no such thing as a free lunch. The saying was an economic maxim by 1938, and Milton Friedman used a version of it as a book title in 1975.
- **Tested by:**

OpenStax makes the same point about time with its missed-class example. ## Does International Trade Create Winners and Losers? (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, Page One Economics)

- **Source:** `source.stlouisfed_trade_winners_losers`
- **URL:** https://www.stlouisfed.org/publications/page-one-economics/2017/11/01/does-international-trade-create-winners-and-losers
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.how_money_works.trade_both_better_off`: unverified

> **Claim:** For a voluntary trade to happen, it must make both parties better off, which makes trade a positive-sum game.

- **Concept:** Gains from trade (`concept.how_money_works.trade_gains`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L71 “Why Countries Trade” · `card.how_money_works.071.c2` (text): Both sides win, or it doesn't happen / Nobody forces a voluntary trade. It happens only if it makes both parties better off: you hand over something you value less for something you value more. Economists call that positive-sum. The swap doesn't just move value around; it creates some. The logic is the same in a school cafeteria and in the global marketplace. Countries don't trade to beat each other. They trade because each side comes out ahead.
  - L73 “Imports and Exports” · `card.how_money_works.073.c4` (fact): Is a trade deficit a loss? People disagree. / Some policymakers see a deficit as proof that a country is losing at trade. Most experts say a deficit, or a surplus, is in itself neither good nor bad. Remember Level 71: each trade happens because both sides expect to gain. Whether a country's overall deficit is a problem is a separate, and still debated, question.
- **Tested by:**
  - L71 `question.how_money_works.071.q1`: When does a voluntary trade take place? → **When both sides expect to be better off**
  - L72 `question.how_money_works.072.q3`: From Level 71: trade happens only when both sides gain. What does England gain from trading with Portugal? → **More wine and more cloth than it could make alone**
  - L73 `question.how_money_works.073.q3`: Level 71 said voluntary trades make both sides better off. What do most experts say about a trade deficit in itself? → **It is neither good nor bad**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. St. Louis Fed education page: for trade to occur, the transaction must make both buyer and seller better off, a positive-sum game; CFR: trade is not a zero-sum game. Sources: https://www.stlouisfed.org/education/is-trade-a-zero-sum-game, https://www.cfr.org/education/learn/reading/what-trade-deficit-means

### ☐ `fact.how_money_works.money_three_jobs`: unverified

> **Claim:** Money does three jobs: it is a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value.

- **Concept:** The three jobs of money (`concept.how_money_works.money_three_jobs`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L1 “Money in One Level” · `card.how_money_works.001.c1` (text): In a WWII prison camp, cigarettes became money. Even non-smokers wanted them. / Economist R. A. Radford was a prisoner there, and in 1945 he explained why. Cigarettes were doing the three jobs that make something money. Learn those three jobs and you know what money is.
  - L1 “Money in One Level” · `card.how_money_works.001.c2` (text): Job 1: a way to pay / Trade in the camp began as barter: my jam for your biscuits, if we each wanted what the other had. Then cigarettes took over. Everyone, non-smokers included, would sell for cigarettes, because they could spend them later on something else. That's a medium of exchange: something you accept not to use, but to pass on.
  - L1 “Money in One Level” · `card.how_money_works.001.c3` (text): Job 2: a measure of value / Soon every price in camp was quoted in cigarettes. Prisoners called out offers like "cheese for seven", and laundry cost two cigarettes a garment. Nobody had to work out what cheese was worth in jam. One common unit let anyone compare anything. That's a unit of account, the ruler you measure value with. Yours is probably dollars, euros or pounds. / Cheese: 7 cigarettes · Laundry: 2 a garment
  - L1 “Money in One Level” · `card.how_money_works.001.c4` (fact): Money you can smoke is a risky way to save. / Job 3 is store of value: money should keep until you're ready to spend it. Prisoners did save cigarettes in reserve. The flaw? People also smoked them. When deliveries stopped, stocks ran out and prices fell. The camp's savings had literally gone up in smoke.
  - L2 “Before Money: Barter” · `card.how_money_works.002.c3` (text): No ruler, no savings / Remember Level 1's three jobs? Barter struggles with them. There's no common ruler: without an agreed measure, every swap sets its own terms, and each deal stands on its own. Saving is hard too. Picture a farmer hoping to buy a tractor in six months with strawberries picked today. By then, they're jam at best.
  - L3 “Shells, Salt and Stones” · `card.how_money_works.003.c1` (text): Money has been shells, salt and stone wheels wider than a car. / None of it was silly. Each one did Level 1's jobs well enough that people trusted it. Here's what made three very different moneys work.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: What Money Is” · `card.how_money_works.010.c4` (text): One thread from shells to code / Money kept changing shape: shells and salt, Lydia's stamped coins, China's paper, gold-backed notes, bank records, bitcoin's blockchain. What stayed the same were Level 1's three jobs, and the thing under them all: people accept money because they trust others will too. Money works because people believe it will.
- **Tested by:**
  - L1 `question.how_money_works.001.q1`: Which list names the three jobs money does? → **A way to pay, a measure of value, a way to save**
  - L1 `question.how_money_works.001.q2`: Why would a non-smoker in Radford's camp sell food for cigarettes? → **They could spend the cigarettes later on something else**
  - L1 `question.how_money_works.001.q3`: A café menu lists every item in dollars. Which camp habit did the same job? → **Quoting every price in cigarettes**
  - L10 `question.how_money_works.010.q3`: From Level 1: you put $20 in a drawer to spend next month. Which job is that money doing? → **Store of value**
  - L31 `question.how_money_works.031.q3`: From Level 1: which of money's three jobs is your savings account doing? → **Store of value**
  - L50 `question.how_money_works.050.q6`: Which of Level 1's three jobs of money lets a price act as a message everyone can read? → **Unit of account**
  - L61 `question.how_money_works.061.q3`: Which of Level 1's three jobs of money does inflation undermine most? → **Store of value**
  - L71 `question.how_money_works.071.q3`: From Level 1: Chile sells copper for money, then spends it on Guatemalan coffee. Which job is money doing? → **Medium of exchange**
  - L99 `question.how_money_works.099.q3`: From Level 1: Save More Tomorrow helps people use money for which of its three jobs? → **Store of value**

### ☐ `fact.how_money_works.company_salomon_1892`: unverified

> **Claim:** In 1892, Aron Salomon, a leather boot maker in Whitechapel, London, turned the business he had run as a sole proprietor into a limited company, keeping nearly all of its shares.

- **Concept:** Salomon and the company as a separate person (`concept.how_money_works.company_salomon_case`)

  - L81 “What a Company Is” · `card.how_money_works.081.c1` (text): A bootmaker's company went bust. Did he have to pay its debts? / Aron Salomon made leather boots in London. In 1892 he turned his business into a limited company, and soon afterwards it failed, owing money. The fight over who should pay went all the way to Britain's top court. Its answer still shapes what a company is.
  - L81 “What a Company Is” · `card.how_money_works.081.c2` (text): Three ways to own a business / The simplest business is a sole proprietorship: one owner, who in law is the business. If it runs up debts, the owner owes them personally, with no limit. A partnership is the same deal shared by two or more owners, and in a general partnership every partner is on the hook. Before 1892, Salomon was a sole proprietor. His boots, and his debts, were all his.
  - L90 “Checkpoint: Companies and Work” · `card.how_money_works.090.c3` (timeline): Chapter 9 on the clock: 1776: Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations opens with the division of labor; 1811: Luddites begin smashing stocking frames near Nottingham; 1892: Aron Salomon turns his boot business into a limited company; 1908–1927: The Model T falls from $850 to as little as $260; 1937: GM recognizes the United Auto Workers; Coase publishes "The Nature of the Firm"; 1961: Unimate, the first industrial robot, starts work at General Motors

### ☐ `fact.how_money_works.company_salomon_ruling`: unverified

> **Claim:** Salomon's company soon failed owing money. Its liquidator argued that Salomon should be personally liable, but the House of Lords ruled that the company was a separate person in law.

- **Concept:** Salomon and the company as a separate person (`concept.how_money_works.company_salomon_case`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L81 “What a Company Is” · `card.how_money_works.081.c1` (text): A bootmaker's company went bust. Did he have to pay its debts? / Aron Salomon made leather boots in London. In 1892 he turned his business into a limited company, and soon afterwards it failed, owing money. The fight over who should pay went all the way to Britain's top court. Its answer still shapes what a company is.
  - L81 “What a Company Is” · `card.how_money_works.081.c3` (text): A person made of paperwork / A corporation is different. In law it's a separate person: it can own property, sign contracts, and sue or be sued. Its owners have limited liability, so they can lose what they put in, but no more. That was the whole case. Salomon's company failed, and its liquidator argued that Salomon should pay its debts himself. The House of Lords said no: the company was a separate person in law, even though he held nearly all its shares.
- **Tested by:**
  - L81 `question.how_money_works.081.q2`: Why didn't Salomon have to pay his failed company's debts himself? → **The company was a separate person in law**
  - L81 `question.how_money_works.081.q3`: Suppose Salomon had never formed a company. Who would have owed his business debts? → **Salomon himself, as a sole proprietor**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Case summaries report that after boot sales declined the company became insolvent, the liquidator sought to make Salomon personally liable, and the House of Lords unanimously upheld the company's separate legal personality. ### ☐ `fact.how_money_works.income_factor_payments`: unverified

> **Claim:** Each factor of production earns its own kind of income: land earns rent, labor earns wages, capital earns interest and entrepreneurship earns profit.

- **Concept:** Four kinds of income (`concept.how_money_works.income_factor_payments`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L11 “Where Income Comes From” · `card.how_money_works.011.c1` (text): One slice of pizza pays four different kinds of income. / The cook, the landlord, the lender behind the oven and the owner of the shop all get a cut of what you paid. Economists have a name for each cut. Learn the four and you'll start seeing them everywhere.
  - L11 “Where Income Comes From” · `card.how_money_works.011.c3` (text): Every ingredient gets paid / Each factor earns its own kind of income. Land earns rent. Labor earns wages. Capital earns interest. Entrepreneurship earns profit, and profit is whatever is left after the wages, rent and interest have been paid. In the pizza shop, the owner gets paid last. / Land: rent · Labor: wages · Capital: interest · Entrepreneurship: profit
  - L11 “Where Income Comes From” · `card.how_money_works.011.c4` (fact): For most people, the paycheck that matters is wages. / Rent goes to people who own land, interest to people who lend, profit to people who own a business. Wages go to anyone who sells their work, and they're the largest source of income for most people. Remember Level 8? Most people now receive that pay as bank deposits, and many never swap it back into cash.
  - L20 “Checkpoint: Earning and Spending” · `card.how_money_works.020.c4` (text): Chapter 2 in one paycheck / Follow one paycheck. It starts as wages, the income labor earns. Deductions shrink gross pay to net. A 50/30/20 budget splits the net into needs, wants and saving, and every choice gives up the next best thing. At the till, price cues nudge you, card fees hide inside prices, small charges quietly add up, and scammers pretend, press and ask for gift cards.

  - L12 `question.how_money_works.012.q3`: From Level 11: gross pay comes from wages. Which factor of production earns wages? → **Labor**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. St. Louis Fed lists rent for land, wages for labor, interest for capital and profit for entrepreneurship; tutor2u defines the same four factor incomes. ### ☐ `fact.how_money_works.nixon_1971_gold_window`: unverified

- **Concept:** Leaving the gold standard (`concept.how_money_works.gold_standard_end`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L7 “The Gold Standard” · `card.how_money_works.007.c1` (text): For generations, a paper note was a ticket you could cash in for gold. / Hand over your notes, walk away with metal. Then, country by country, the deal ended. The last big link snapped on August 15, 1971.
  - L7 “The Gold Standard” · `card.how_money_works.007.c4` (fact): In 1971, Nixon "temporarily" cut the dollar's last link to gold. / After World War II, the Bretton Woods system fixed other currencies to the dollar, and dollars to gold at $35 an ounce.
